**Apple Inc.** is an American multinational [technology company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_company "Technology company") headquartered in [Cupertino, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupertino,_California "Cupertino, California"), in [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley"), and known for consumer electronics, software and online services. Founded in 1976 as Apple Computer Company by [Steve Jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs"), Steve Wozniak and [Ronald Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Wayne "Ronald Wayne"), the company was incorporated by Jobs and Wozniak as Apple Computer, Inc. the following year. Its current name was adopted in 2007 as the company expanded its focus from computers to consumer electronics. Apple is one of the [Big Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech "Big Tech") companies.

The company was founded to market Wozniak's [Apple I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_I "Apple I") computer. Its successor, the [Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_(original) "Apple II (original)"), became one of the first successful mass-produced personal [microcomputers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microcomputer "Microcomputer"). Apple introduced the [Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Lisa "Apple Lisa") in 1983 and the [Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_128K "Macintosh 128K") in 1984, popularizing [graphical user interfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") navigated by a [mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_mouse "Computer mouse"). By 1985, internal conflicts led to Jobs leaving the company to form [NeXT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NeXT "NeXT") and Wozniak stepping back from active employment. During the 1990s, Apple lost considerable market share to lower-priced [Wintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wintel "Wintel") computers, [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel")-powered [PC clones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC_clones "PC clones") running [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows "Windows"). By 1997, Apple was reporting major losses and struggling to deliver a modernized operating system, leading it to acquire NeXT, which brought Jobs back to the company. Under his leadership, Apple returned to profitability through the [iMac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMac "IMac"), [iPod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPod "IPod"), [iPhone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone "IPhone"), and [iPad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPad "IPad"), the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store"), the [Apple Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Store "Apple Store") retail chain, and the "[Think different](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_different "Think different")" advertising campaign. Jobs resigned in 2011 for health reasons and died later that year.

[Apple's product lineup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Apple_products "List of Apple products") includes portable and home hardware like the iPhone, iPad, [Mac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_(computer) "Mac (computer)"), [Apple Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Watch "Apple Watch"), and [AirPods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AirPods "AirPods"); [several in-house operating systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Apple_operating_systems "List of Apple operating systems") such as [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS"), [iPadOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPadOS "IPadOS"), and [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS "MacOS"); and [various software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_software_by_Apple "List of software by Apple") and services including [Apple Pay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Pay "Apple Pay") and [iCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICloud "ICloud"), as well as multimedia streaming services like [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music") and [Apple TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_TV_(streaming_service) "Apple TV (streaming service)"). Since 2011, Apple has for the most part been the world's [largest company by market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_public_corporations_by_market_capitalization "List of public corporations by market capitalization"), and, as of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Apple_Inc.&action=edit), is the [largest manufacturing company by revenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_manufacturing_companies_by_revenue "List of largest manufacturing companies by revenue"), the [fourth-largest PC vendor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_share_of_personal_computer_vendors#Current_top_vendors_market_share_(2023) "Market share of personal computer vendors"), the [largest vendor of tablet computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablet_computer#By_manufacturer "Tablet computer"), and the [largest vendor of mobile phones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_mobile_phones#2024 "List of best-selling mobile phones"). Apple became the first publicly traded US company to be [valued at over $1 trillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trillion-dollar_company "Trillion-dollar company") in 2018, and, as of October 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Apple_Inc.&action=edit), is valued at just over $4 trillion.

[Apple has received criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criticism_of_Apple_Inc. "Criticism of Apple Inc.") regarding [its contractors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_supply_chain "Apple supply chain")' labor conditions, [its relationship with trade unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc._and_unions "Apple Inc. and unions"), [its environmental practices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_of_Apple_Inc. "Environmental impact of Apple Inc."), and its corporate ethics, including [anti-competitive tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-competitive_practices_of_Apple_Inc. "Anti-competitive practices of Apple Inc."), materials sourcing, and [its acquisitions of smaller businesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mergers_and_acquisitions_by_Apple "List of mergers and acquisitions by Apple"). Nevertheless, the company has [a large following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_community "Apple community") and enjoys [a high level of customer loyalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing_of_Apple_Inc.#Brand_loyalty "Marketing of Apple Inc."). Apple has consistently been ranked as one of the world's [most valuable brands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_valuable_brands "List of most valuable brands") since the late 2000s.

## History

Main article: [History of Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Apple_Inc. "History of Apple Inc.")

### 1976–1984: Founding and incorporation

See also: [List of Mac models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Mac_models "List of Mac models") and [Timeline of the Apple II family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Apple_II_family "Timeline of the Apple II family")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Apple_Garage.jpg/250px-Apple_Garage.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_Garage.jpg)

In 1976, [Steve Jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs") and Steve Wozniak co-founded Apple in Jobs' parents' home in [Los Altos, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Altos,_California "Los Altos, California").

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/CopsonApple1_2k_cropped.jpg/250px-CopsonApple1_2k_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CopsonApple1_2k_cropped.jpg)

The [Apple I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_I "Apple I"), the company's first product, was sold as an assembled board without a keyboard, power supply, or case.

Apple Computer Company was founded as a [partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership "Partnership") on April 1, 1976, by [Steve Jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs"), Steve Wozniak, and [Ronald Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Wayne "Ronald Wayne").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer20046%E2%80%938-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-6) The company's first product was the [Apple I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_I "Apple I"), designed by Wozniak and hand-built.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-7) To finance production, Jobs sold his [Volkswagen Bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volkswagen_Type_2 "Volkswagen Type 2") and Wozniak sold his [HP-65](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HP-65 "HP-65") calculator. Although neither received the full selling price, together they raised $1,300(equivalent to $7,400 in 2025).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-8)

Wozniak demonstrated the first Apple I prototype at the [Homebrew Computer Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homebrew_Computer_Club "Homebrew Computer Club") in July 1976, where local computer retailer [Byte Shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byte_Shop "Byte Shop") placed an order for 50 fully assembled computers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Freiberger2000-10) Unlike most contemporary hobbyist computers, which were sold as kits requiring assembly, the Apple I came as a pre-assembled [motherboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motherboard "Motherboard") with a [CPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPU "CPU"), [RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAM "RAM"), and built-in video circuitry, allowing it to connect directly to a household television instead of requiring a costly computer terminal. Users still had to provide a case, power supply, and keyboard. It was introduced at a price of $666.66(equivalent to $3,770 in 2025).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWozniakSmith2006180-12)

Apple Computer, Inc. was incorporated in [Cupertino, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupertino,_California "Cupertino, California"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Apple-10-K-Report-2025-1) on January 3, 1977,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200410-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Apple_FAQ-14) without Wayne, who had left and sold his share of the company back to Jobs and Wozniak for $800(equivalent to $4,530 in 2025) twelve days after its founding.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-15) Multimillionaire [Mike Markkula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Markkula "Mike Markkula") provided business expertise and invested $250,000(equivalent to $1,328,000 in 2025) during the company's incorporation.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-16) During its first five years, revenue grew rapidly, doubling approximately every four months. Between September 1977 and September 1980, annual sales increased from $775,000 to 118 million, an average annual growth rate of 533%.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-17)

The [Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_(1977_computer) "Apple II (1977 computer)"), also designed by Wozniak, was introduced on April 16, 1977, at the first [West Coast Computer Faire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_Computer_Faire "West Coast Computer Faire").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200412-18) Alongside the [Commodore PET 2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_PET_2001 "Commodore PET 2001") and the [TRS-80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRS-80 "TRS-80"), it formed the "[1977 Trinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_Trinity "1977 Trinity")" of influential personal computers that established the home computer market. Unlike the Apple I, the Apple II was mass-produced as a complete personal computer housed in a plastic case with a built-in keyboard, color graphics, and an [open architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_architecture "Open architecture").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200412%E2%80%9315-19) Apple introduced the [Disk II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_II "Disk II")5+1⁄4-inch floppy disk drive in 1978, replacing cassette tape storage with faster and more reliable removable disks.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200413%E2%80%9315-20)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Apple_II_Plus_cropped.jpg/250px-Apple_II_Plus_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_II_Plus_cropped.jpg)

The [Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"), introduced in 1977, became Apple's first commercially successful computer.

The Apple II became Apple's first major commercial success following the 1979 release of [VisiCalc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisiCalc "VisiCalc"), the first widely adopted [spreadsheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spreadsheet "Spreadsheet") program and one of the earliest personal computer "[killer applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killer_application "Killer application")". Initially available exclusively for the Apple II, VisiCalc transformed the computer into a popular business tool and helped establish Apple in the growing personal computer industry.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200413%E2%80%9315-20)

On December 12, 1980, Apple became a public company through an [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO) on the [Nasdaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdaq "Nasdaq"). The company sold 4.6 million shares at $22 each,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Apple_FAQ2-21) raising more than $100 million, the largest IPO since [Ford Motor Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company")'s 1956 offering.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-EDNAAPLSTOCK2-22) By the end of the first day of trading, Apple's [market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") reached $1.778 billion and more than 300 employees and investors became millionaires.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-EDNAAPLSTOCK2-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-DEDIPO2-23)

In November and December 1979, Apple employees, including Jobs and [Jef Raskin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jef_Raskin "Jef Raskin"), visited [Xerox PARC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerox_PARC "Xerox PARC") twice as part of a technology exchange negotiated by Jobs, in which [Xerox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerox "Xerox") was granted the right to purchase $1 million of Apple's pre-IPO stock.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIsaacson201596%E2%80%9397-24) There they observed the experimental [Xerox Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerox_Alto "Xerox Alto"), which featured a [graphical user interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") (GUI) navigated with a [mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_mouse "Computer mouse"), that inspired Jobs to incorporate a GUI into Apple's future products.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200474%E2%80%9375-25) Apple's first GUI-based computer, the [Apple Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Lisa "Apple Lisa"), was introduced in 1983. Although the Lisa was pioneering as a mass-marketed GUI computer, its high price and limited software library resulted in poor sales.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200468-26)

Jobs was removed from the Lisa project during its early development and joined the [Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh "Macintosh") division in 1981. The Macintosh had originally been conceived by Raskin as a low-cost, [portable computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portable_computer "Portable computer"), with early contributions from Wozniak. After Wozniak stepped back following a plane crash, Jobs took over the project,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer200428,_86%E2%80%9388-28) transforming the Macintosh into a mouse-driven computer with a GUI similar to the Lisa. Wozniak later speculated that Jobs' rivalry with the Lisa project was the driving force behind this shift in direction.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-TheVerge-29) Jobs was also hostile toward the Apple II division, which at the time generated most of the company's revenue.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-rice19850415-30)

### 1984–1991: Success with Macintosh

See also: [List of Mac models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Mac_models "List of Mac models")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Steve_Jobs_and_Macintosh_computer%2C_January_1984%2C_by_Bernard_Gotfryd_-_edited.jpg/250px-Steve_Jobs_and_Macintosh_computer%2C_January_1984%2C_by_Bernard_Gotfryd_-_edited.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Steve_Jobs_and_Macintosh_computer,_January_1984,_by_Bernard_Gotfryd_-_edited.jpg)

[Steve Jobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs") in 1984 with the [Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_128k "Macintosh 128k"), the first successful mass-market personal computer to feature an integral [graphical user interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") and [mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_mouse "Computer mouse")

In 1984, Apple launched [the original Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_128K "Macintosh 128K") on January 24, 1984, introducing it to the public with "[1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_(advertisement) "1984 (advertisement)")", a US$1.5-million television advertisement directed by [Ridley Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridley_Scott "Ridley Scott") that aired during the third quarter of [Super Bowl XVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XVIII "Super Bowl XVIII") on January 22, 1984.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-31) This was hailed as a watershed event for Apple's success[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-32) and was called a "masterpiece" by [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN")[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-33) and one of "the greatest TV commercials of all time" by _[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV\_Guide "TV Guide")_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-34) Although initial Macintosh sales were strong, they declined rapidly after the first few months as reviewers criticized its limited 128 KB of RAM, small software library, and relatively high price of $2,495(equivalent to $7,700 in 2025).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-35)

Slow Macintosh sales led to a power struggle between Jobs and chief executive officer [John Sculley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Sculley "John Sculley"), whom Jobs had recruited from [PepsiCo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PepsiCo "PepsiCo") in 1983.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-36) The board of directors instructed Sculley to limit Jobs' ability to launch further expensive forays into untested products. Rather than accept Sculley's direction, Jobs attempted to remove him as chief executive.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004156%E2%80%93157-37)[Jean-Louis Gassée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Louis_Gass%C3%A9e "Jean-Louis Gassée") informed Sculley of Jobs' efforts to organize a [boardroom coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boardroom_coup "Boardroom coup"), prompting an emergency meeting in which Apple's executive staff sided with Sculley. In May 1985, the board stripped Jobs of all operational duties.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004156%E2%80%93157-37) Jobs resigned from Apple in September 1985 and founded competitor [NeXT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NeXT "NeXT"), taking several Apple employees with him.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-38)

Wozniak had already stepped away from day-to-day operations following a 1981 plane crash. He left active employment at Apple in 1985, citing frustration that the company was prioritizing the Macintosh over the Apple II division, which continued to generate a significant portion of Apple's revenue during the mid-1980s.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-39) He remained an Apple shareholder and continued to represent the company in a ceremonial capacity.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-rice198504152-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-wozemployee2-41)

After the departures of Jobs and Wozniak in 1985, Sculley shifted Apple's focus toward expanding the Macintosh platform and appointed Gassée to lead Macintosh development, placing him in the role previously held by Jobs. That year, Apple introduced the [LaserWriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaserWriter "LaserWriter") in March, one of the first affordable [PostScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PostScript "PostScript")-based laser printers, while [Aldus Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldus_Corporation "Aldus Corporation") introduced [PageMaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PageMaker "PageMaker") in July.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004158%E2%80%93159-42) The combination of the Macintosh, LaserWriter, and PageMaker helped establish the [desktop publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_publishing "Desktop publishing") market.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-43)

In March 1987, Apple introduced the [Macintosh II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_II "Macintosh II"), a modular computer with a separate monitor. It was the first Macintosh to support color graphics and feature internal expansion slots, broadening the platform's capabilities beyond the original all-in-one design.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Macworld_2026-44)

Apple's success in desktop publishing allowed the company to pursue a premium pricing strategy,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaine2014359%E2%80%93363-45) sometimes referred to as the "high-right policy" because of its position on a price–profitability chart. Under this strategy, Apple focused on higher-[margin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profit_margin "Profit margin") products rather than competing on price, with executives believing that [power users](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_user "Power user") would continue to pay for increased performance and capabilities. The policy was championed by Gassée, who promoted a target Macintosh profit margin of 55 percent.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarlton199779%E2%80%9380-46) Gassée also opposed proposals to license the [Mac OS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_OS "Mac OS") to other manufacturers.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-lemms-47)

By 1988, Gassée was viewed by some as a potential successor to Sculley, however, the "high-right policy" he championed began to lose ground as desktop publishing software became available on [IBM PC compatible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") computers that sold at lower prices. For the first time in the company's history, sales declined in the 1989 holiday season, followed by a 20 percent drop in Apple's stock price.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarlton1997117%E2%80%93129-48) In January 1990, Sculley appointed [Michael Spindler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Spindler "Michael Spindler") as [chief operating officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_operating_officer "Chief operating officer"), reducing Gassée's influence.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004184%E2%80%93185-49) Gassée left Apple at the end of 1990 and founded competitor [Be Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Be_Inc. "Be Inc.") in 1991, taking several Apple employees with him.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004160-50)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Apple_Museum_%28Prague%29_Macintosh_LC_%281990%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Apple_Museum_%28Prague%29_Macintosh_LC_%281990%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_Museum_(Prague)_Macintosh_LC_(1990)_(cropped).jpg)

[Macintosh LC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_LC "Macintosh LC")

The company shifted its product strategy and, in October 1990, introduced three lower-cost models: the [Macintosh Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_Classic "Macintosh Classic"), [LC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_LC "Macintosh LC"), and [IIsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IIsi "IIsi"), all of which sold well.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004128-51) In 1991, Apple introduced the [PowerBook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerBook_100_series "PowerBook 100 series") line of laptop computers, whose design influenced nearly all future laptops by placing the keyboard behind a built-in [pointing device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointing_device "Pointing device"), creating palm rests. The PowerBook was commercially successful, capturing about 40 percent of the notebook computer market during its first year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Macworld_2026-44) The same year, Apple introduced [System 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_7 "System 7"), a major upgrade to the Macintosh operating system that introduced a color user interface and improved networking capabilities. The success of the lower-priced Macintosh models and the PowerBook contributed to increased revenue.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-lemsculley-52)_[MacAddict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacAddict "MacAddict")_ later described the period from 1989 to 1991 as the Macintosh's "first golden age".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-53)

### 1991–1997: Decline and increased competition

However, the success of the lower-cost Macintosh models also cannibalized sales of Apple's high-end systems. In response, the company introduced several new brands, selling largely identical machines at different price points, for different markets: the high-end [Quadra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_Quadra "Macintosh Quadra") series, the mid-range [Centris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_Centris "Macintosh Centris"), and the consumer-oriented [Performa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performa "Performa"). This led to widespread consumer confusion.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-vawperforma-54) Apple discontinued the Apple II in 1993 after encouraging developers and customers to transition to the Macintosh, bringing the company's longest-running product line to an end.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-56)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Apple_Newton_MessagePad_100_with_stylus.jpg/250px-Apple_Newton_MessagePad_100_with_stylus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_Newton_MessagePad_100_with_stylus.jpg)

Newton [MessagePad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MessagePad "MessagePad") with stylus

During the 1990s, Apple also branched out beyond computers, developing several consumer products, among them the [QuickTake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QuickTake "QuickTake") digital cameras, [PowerCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerCD "PowerCD"), [Pippin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Pippin "Apple Pippin") game console, [eWorld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EWorld "EWorld") online service, [Apple Interactive Television Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Interactive_Television_Box "Apple Interactive Television Box"), and the [Apple Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Newton "Apple Newton") PDA line. Although technologically ambitious, none achieved commercial success.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-57)

Meanwhile, Microsoft expanded the reach of [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows "Windows") by focusing on inexpensive personal computers, while Apple continued to emphasize premium hardware with high profit margins.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-58)[Apple unsuccessfully sued Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Computer,_Inc._v._Microsoft_Corp. "Apple Computer, Inc. v. Microsoft Corp.") over similarities between Windows and the Lisa operating system.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-lemms-47) The consumer product flops and the rapid loss of market share to Windows sullied Apple's reputation, and in 1993 Sculley was replaced as CEO by Michael Spindler.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-59)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/PowerMac_6100-66b.JPG/250px-PowerMac_6100-66b.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PowerMac_6100-66b.JPG)

[Power Macintosh 6100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_Macintosh_6100 "Power Macintosh 6100"), Apple's first computer with a [PowerPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC "PowerPC") processor, introduced in 1994

In 1994, Apple, [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"), and [Motorola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola "Motorola") formed the [AIM alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIM_alliance "AIM alliance") to promote the [PowerPC platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC_Reference_Platform "PowerPC Reference Platform"). That year, Apple introduced the first [Power Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_Macintosh "Power Macintosh") models using [PowerPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC "PowerPC") processors.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-60) In the wake of the alliance, Apple opened up to the idea of allowing Motorola and other companies to build [Macintosh clones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_clone "Macintosh clone"). Over the next two years, 75 distinct Macintosh clone models were introduced. However, by 1996, Apple executives were worried that the clones were cannibalizing sales of its own high-end computers, where profit margins were highest.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinzmayer2004[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidmXnw5tM8QRwCpgPA254_254%E2%80%93256]-61)

Spindler's tenure was also marked by repeated attempts to modernize the [Macintosh operating system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Mac_OS "Classic Mac OS"). The original [System 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_1 "System 1") was not built for [multitasking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_multitasking "Computer multitasking") (running several applications at once), and although Apple introduced [cooperative multitasking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_multitasking "Cooperative multitasking") in System 5, the company concluded that a more modern approach was needed.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-62) Internal efforts, including [Pink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taligent "Taligent"), [A/UX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A/UX "A/UX"), and [Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copland_(operating_system) "Copland (operating system)"), failed to produce a suitable successor, with Copland falling well behind schedule before being abandoned.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-AppleConfidential-64):273–274

In 1996, Spindler was replaced as CEO by [Gil Amelio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Amelio "Gil Amelio"), who was hired for his reputation as a corporate rehabilitator. Amelio made big changes, including extensive layoffs and cost-cutting.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-65) Amelio began evaluating external operating systems, including [Windows NT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_NT "Windows NT") and [Solaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solaris_(operating_system) "Solaris (operating system)"), before entering negotiations to acquire Be Inc. and its [BeOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BeOS "BeOS") operating system.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-66) The talks ultimately collapsed amid disagreements over the company's valuation, with Be seeking substantially more than Apple was willing to pay. Gassée later disputed that the negotiations failed solely over price, stating that disagreements over his prospective role at Apple also contributed to the breakdown.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-67)

Apple instead acquired NeXT, the company founded by Steve Jobs, for its NeXTSTEP operating system. Apple purchased NeXT for $427 million in cash, stock, stock options, and assumed debt.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-AppleConfidential-64):277[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-68) At the insistence of Amelio, Jobs accepted 1.5 million Apple shares to lend credibility to the deal and agreed to return to Apple as an advisor.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-70)

### 1997–2007: Restructuring and return to profitability

The NeXT acquisition was completed on February 7, 1997.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-archive-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Linzmayer1999-72) Jobs quickly became frustrated with the leadership of Amelio and Apple's board. In June 1997, he anonymously sold his 1.5 million shares, sending the company's stock price lower and contributing to pressure on Amelio, whom the board ousted the following month.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-73) Jobs became Apple's _de facto_ leader and was formally appointed interim CEO on September 16.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Entrepreneur20111027-75)

In August 1997, Jobs secured a $150 million investment from Microsoft and a commitment to continue developing software for the Mac platform,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-76) an agreement widely viewed as beneficial to both companies following [Microsoft's antitrust settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Microsoft_Corp. "United States v. Microsoft Corp.") with the U.S. Department of Justice.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-77) Jobs ended the Macintosh clone licensing program, and in September 1997, acquired the largest clone manufacturer, [Power Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_Computing "Power Computing").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-78) In November 1997, the [online Apple Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Store_(online) "Apple Store (online)") launched and adopted a build-to-order manufacturing model similar to that used by [Dell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dell "Dell").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-79) By the end of 1997, Jobs had returned Apple to profitability, reporting a profit of $309 million.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Entrepreneur20111027-75)

Jobs streamlined Apple's product lineup, eliminating roughly 70 percent of existing models and introducing a simplified 'four-quadrant' product strategy consisting of one desktop and one laptop computer each for consumer and professional markets.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-80) The restructuring eliminated approximately 3,000 jobs.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Entrepreneur20111027-75)

The first all-new product introduced under this strategy was the [iMac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMac_G3 "IMac G3"), unveiled on May 6, 1998. Designed by [Jony Ive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jony_Ive "Jony Ive"), the all-in-one computer featured a distinctive translucent design enclosure, emphasized Internet connectivity (the "i" in iMac), adopted modern technologies such as [USB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USB "USB"), and omitted legacy technologies like the [floppy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk") drive. It sold approximately 800,000 units within its first five months on the market.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-800kimacs-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Alyson_Raletz-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Time-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-84)

Apple completed the transition to the four-quadrant lineup on July 21, 1999, with the introduction of the consumer-oriented [iBook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBook "IBook") laptop. It joined the iMac and updated [G3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC_7xx "PowerPC 7xx")-powered versions of the professional [Power Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_Macintosh_G3 "Power Macintosh G3") desktop and [PowerBook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerBook_G3 "PowerBook G3") laptop, completing the simplified product matrix. Jobs said the smaller product lineup allowed Apple to focus more on quality and innovation.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-85)

During this period, Apple also focused on building an ecosystem around digital media, similar to its earlier efforts in desktop publishing, through a series of acquisitions and product launches. Apple acquired [Macromedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macromedia "Macromedia")'s Key Grip digital video editing project, which became [Final Cut Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Cut_Pro "Final Cut Pro") in April 1999.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-86) The technology also contributed to the development of [iMovie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMovie "IMovie"), Apple's consumer video-editing application, released in October 1999.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Bell-87) In April 2000, Apple acquired German company [Astarte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astarte "Astarte"), whose DVDirector [DVD authoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD_authoring "DVD authoring") software was repackaged as [DVD Studio Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD_Studio_Pro "DVD Studio Pro") for professionals and adapted into [iDVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDVD "IDVD") for consumers.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Bell-87) Later that year, Apple acquired [SoundJam MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoundJam_MP "SoundJam MP") from [Casady & Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casady_&_Greene "Casady & Greene") and relaunched it as [iTunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes "ITunes"), adding a simplified interface and CD-burning capabilities.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-88)

In 2001, Apple made three announcements that would shape its future direction. On March 24, Apple released [Mac OS X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_OS_X "Mac OS X"), its next-generation operating system after years of failed attempts to modernize the classic Mac OS. Based on [NeXTSTEP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NeXTSTEP "NeXTSTEP"), Mac OS X combined a stable, reliable, and secure Unix foundation with a redesigned GUI. In May, Apple opened its first two [Apple Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Store "Apple Store") retail locations in [McLean, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLean,_Virginia "McLean, Virginia"), and [Glendale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale,_California "Glendale, California"), providing controlled spaces to showcase its products and services.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-First_stores-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-MacRumors_stores-91) Despite skepticism that it would be able to compete as a retailer, the stores succeeded, and Apple expanded to more than 500 locations worldwide.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-fortune-best-retailer-92)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-storelist-2) On November 10, Apple released the [iPod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPod "IPod"), its first major consumer product outside the computer market in years. The portable digital audio player became a major success, selling more than 100 million units within six years.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-93)

In 2002, Apple acquired [Nothing Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothing_Real "Nothing Real") for its digital [compositing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compositing "Compositing") application [Shake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_(software) "Shake (software)"),[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-94) and [Emagic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emagic "Emagic"), developer of the music production software [Logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_Pro "Logic Pro"). The acquisition made Apple the first computer manufacturer to own a music software company and was followed by the development of the consumer-oriented [GarageBand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GarageBand "GarageBand") application.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-95) In 2002, Apple also introduced [iPhoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhoto "IPhoto"), completing the [iLife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ILife "ILife") software suite.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-96)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/ITunes_Store_Songs_Sales.jpg/250px-ITunes_Store_Songs_Sales.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ITunes_Store_Songs_Sales.jpg)

The iTunes Store was highly successful in shaping the legal [music downloading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download") industry; chart shows the number of songs sold from 2003 to 2010.

In 2003, Apple launched the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store"), allowing customers to purchase and [download music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Download_music "Download music") for 99¢ per song. The service quickly became the leading online music retailer, reaching more than 5 billion downloads by June 2008 and becoming the world's largest music retailer two years later.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-98) The iTunes Store helped transform the music industry by shifting consumers from unauthorized file-sharing services such as [Napster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napster "Napster") toward paid digital distribution.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Macworld_2026-44)

In January 2005, Apple introduced the [Mac Mini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_Mini "Mac Mini"), a low-cost computer intended to attract Windows users. It was priced starting at US$499(equivalent to $800 in 2025) with users expected to re-use their existing display, keyboard, and mouse.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-Macworld_2026-44)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/MacBook_Pro.jpg/250px-MacBook_Pro.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MacBook_Pro.jpg)

[MacBook Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacBook_Pro "MacBook Pro"), Apple's first laptop with an [Intel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel "Intel") processor, introduced in 2006

At the [Worldwide Developers Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worldwide_Developers_Conference "Worldwide Developers Conference") on June 6, 2005, Jobs announced that Apple would [transition the Mac from PowerPC to Intel processors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_transition_to_Intel_processors "Mac transition to Intel processors") over the following two years.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-printel-99) The first Intel-based Macs, the [MacBook Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacBook_Pro "MacBook Pro") and [iMac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMac_(Intel-based) "IMac (Intel-based)"), were introduced on January 10, 2006, using Intel's [Core Duo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel_Core_(microarchitecture)#Yonah "Intel Core (microarchitecture)") processors. Apple completed the transition on August 7, 2006, approximately one year ahead of its announced schedule.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-printel-99) During the transition, the Power Mac, iBook, and PowerBook brands were retired and replaced by the [Mac Pro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_Pro "Mac Pro"), [MacBook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacBook "MacBook"), and MacBook Pro.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-100) Apple also introduced [Boot Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boot_Camp_(software) "Boot Camp (software)") in 2006, allowing users to install Windows on Intel-based Macs alongside Mac OS X.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-101)

Between 2003 and 2006, the price of Apple's stock increased more than tenfold, from around $6 per share ([split-adjusted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-adjusted "Split-adjusted")) to over $80.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-102) When Apple surpassed Dell's [market cap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_cap "Market cap") in January 2006,[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-modell-103) Jobs sent an email to Apple employees saying [Michael Dell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Dell "Michael Dell") should eat his words,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-104) referencing his 1997 remark that, if he ran Apple, he would "shut it down and give the money back to the shareholders".[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-105)

### 2007–2011: Success with mobile devices

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/IPhone_%28356419153%29.jpg/250px-IPhone_%28356419153%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IPhone_(356419153).jpg)

The newly announced [first-generation iPhone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_(1st_generation) "IPhone (1st generation)") was on display at the 2007 [MacWorld Expo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacWorld_Expo "MacWorld Expo").

During his keynote at the [Macworld Expo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macworld_Expo "Macworld Expo") on January 9, 2007, Jobs announced that Apple Computer, Inc. would be renamed Apple Inc. to reflect the company's expanded focus on consumer electronics.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-106) He also introduced the [Apple TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_TV_(device) "Apple TV (device)") and the [iPhone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone "IPhone").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-107)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-108) The iPhone had been [developed in secret since 2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_iPhone "History of the iPhone") and was the subject of widespread speculation before its introduction. Jobs presented it as a device that combined the functions of an iPod, a mobile phone, and an Internet communications device. Unlike most contemporary mobile phones, it used a finger-operated [multi-touch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-touch "Multi-touch") interface and eliminated most physical buttons. Released in the United States on June 29, 2007, the iPhone sold 270,000 units within 30 hours of release.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-109)

In an open letter published on February 6, 2007, Jobs said Apple favored selling music on the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") without [FairPlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FairPlay "FairPlay"), its [digital rights management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_rights_management "Digital rights management") (DRM) technology, if record labels agreed to remove DRM from their music catalogs.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-110) On April 2, 2007, [EMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI "EMI") announced that DRM would be removed from its catalog beginning in May 2007.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-111) Other record labels later followed suit, and Apple announced in January 2009 that all songs were available without DRM.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-112)

In July 2008, Apple launched the [App Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/App_Store_(iOS) "App Store (iOS)") for third-party iPhone applications.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-113) Within a month, the store had sold 60 million applications and generated average daily revenue of $1 million. Jobs said the App Store could become a billion-dollar business for Apple.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-114)

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/IPod_classic_in_dock.jpg/250px-IPod_classic_in_dock.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IPod_classic_in_dock.jpg)

A docked [iPod Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPod_Classic "IPod Classic"); Apple worked with other manufacturers to implement purpose-built "[Made for iPod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made_for_iPod "Made for iPod")" docking stations.

On January 14, 2009, Jobs announced that he would take a six-month medical [leave of absence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leave_of_absence "Leave of absence") through the end of June to focus on his health.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-115) During his absence, Apple reported revenue of $8.16 billion and profit of $1.21 billion for its first fiscal quarter of 2009.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-116)

Apple introduced the [iPad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPad "IPad") on January 27, 2010. It ran the same touch-based operating system as the iPhone and supported existing iPhone applications. Released in the United States on April 3, 2010, the iPad sold more than 300,000 units on its first day and more than 500,000 during its first week.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-117) In May 2010, Apple's market capitalization exceeded Microsoft's for the first time since 1989.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-118)

On January 17, 2011, Jobs announced in an internal Apple memo that he would take another indefinite medical leave to focus on his health. Chief operating officer [Tim Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Cook "Tim Cook") assumed responsibility for Apple's day-to-day operations while Jobs remained involved in major strategic decisions.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-JobsLeave2011-119) In June 2011, Jobs introduced [iCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICloud "ICloud"), an online storage and synchronization service that replaced [MobileMe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MobileMe "MobileMe").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-120) It was the last Apple product launch presented by Jobs before his death.

On August 24, 2011, Jobs resigned as Apple's chief executive officer because of his health.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-121) Cook succeeded him as CEO,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-122) and Jobs became chairman of Apple, a new position at the company.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-123)[Arthur Levinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Levinson "Arthur Levinson") succeeded Jobs as chairman in November 2011 following Jobs' death.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-124)

### 2011–2020: Post-Jobs era, new devices

On October 5, 2011, Steve Jobs died.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-125) That same month, Apple released the [iPhone 4s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_4s "IPhone 4s"), which introduced [Siri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siri "Siri"), an [intelligent software assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligent_software_assistant "Intelligent software assistant") built into iOS.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-126) On August 20, 2012, Apple's rising stock price increased the company's market capitalization to a then-record $624 billion. This beat the non-inflation-adjusted record for market capitalization previously set by [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") in 1999.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-127)

In May 2014, Apple announced it would acquire [Dr. Dre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Dre "Dr. Dre") and [Jimmy Iovine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Iovine "Jimmy Iovine")'s company [Beats Electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beats_Electronics "Beats Electronics"), the producer of the "Beats by Dr. Dre" headphone line and operator of the [Beats Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beats_Music "Beats Music") streaming service, for US$3 billion. It was the largest acquisition in Apple's history at the time.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-128) At WWDC in June 2015, Apple launched [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music "Apple Music"), a subscription streaming service built on the Beats acquisition.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-129)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Apple_Watch_%E3%81%A7%E3%83%81%E3%82%A7%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%82%A4%E3%83%B3%E3%81%97%E3%81%BE%E3%81%97%E3%81%9F%EF%BC%81_2015_%2817187691969%29.jpg/250px-Apple_Watch_%E3%81%A7%E3%83%81%E3%82%A7%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%82%A4%E3%83%B3%E3%81%97%E3%81%BE%E3%81%97%E3%81%9F%EF%BC%81_2015_%2817187691969%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_Watch_%E3%81%A7%E3%83%81%E3%82%A7%E3%83%83%E3%82%AF%E3%82%A4%E3%83%B3%E3%81%97%E3%81%BE%E3%81%97%E3%81%9F%EF%BC%81_2015_(17187691969).jpg)

[First-generation Apple Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Watch_(1st_generation) "Apple Watch (1st generation)") (2015)

During a press event on September 9, 2014, Apple introduced the [Apple Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Watch "Apple Watch"), its first [smartwatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartwatch "Smartwatch").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-verge-watchannounce2-130) Apple initially marketed the device as a [fashion accessory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion_accessory "Fashion accessory")[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-wp-fashion2-131) and a companion to the iPhone,[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-wired.com2-132) before shifting its focus toward health and fitness features to compete with dedicated [activity trackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activity_trackers "Activity trackers").

In September 2017, Apple released the [iPhone X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_X "IPhone X"), which replaced the physical home button with an edge-to-edge display and introduced [Face ID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_ID "Face ID"), a facial-recognition system that replaced [Touch ID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touch_ID "Touch ID") as the phone's unlock method.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-133) The design set the template for subsequent iPhone models. That same year, in June 2017, Apple announced [HomePod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HomePod "HomePod"), its first [smart speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_speaker "Smart speaker"), aimed at competing with [Sonos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonos "Sonos"), [Google Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Home_(smart_speakers) "Google Home (smart speakers)"), and [Amazon Echo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Echo "Amazon Echo").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-134)

Also in 2017, Apple formed a video unit to produce original television series and films, later marketed as [Apple TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_TV_(streaming_service) "Apple TV (streaming service)"),[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-135) and in June 2018, Apple signed the [Writers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America")'s minimum basic agreement.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-136)

On August 19, 2020, Apple's share price briefly topped $467.77, making it the first US company with a market capitalization of US$2 trillion.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.#cite_note-137)

### 2020–2026: Transition to Apple silicon

1977–1993 series of microcomputers

The **Apple II** (stylized as **apple ][**) is a series of [microcomputers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microcomputer "Microcomputer") manufactured by [Apple Computer, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Computer,_Inc. "Apple Computer, Inc.") from 1977 to 1993. The [original Apple II model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_(original) "Apple II (original)"), which gave the series its name, was designed by Steve Wozniak and was first sold on June 10, 1977.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-Apple_II_intro_date-2) Its success led to it being followed by the [Apple II Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_Plus "Apple II Plus"), [Apple IIe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_IIe "Apple IIe"), [Apple IIc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_IIc "Apple IIc"), and [Apple IIc Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_IIc_Plus "Apple IIc Plus"), with the IIe being the most popular. The name is trademarked with square brackets as Apple][, then, beginning with the IIe, as **Apple//**.

The Apple II was a major advancement over its predecessor, the [Apple I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_I "Apple I"), in terms of ease of use, features, and expandability. It became one of several recognizable and successful computers throughout the 1980s, although this was mainly limited to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). It was aggressively marketed through volume discounts and [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing "Manufacturing") arrangements to educational institutions, which made it the first computer in widespread use in American secondary schools, displacing the early leader [Commodore PET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodore_PET "Commodore PET"). The effort to develop educational and business [software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software "Software") for the Apple II, including the 1979 release of the [VisiCalc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VisiCalc "VisiCalc")[spreadsheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spreadsheet "Spreadsheet"), made the computer especially popular with business users and families.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-5)

The Apple II computers are based on the [6502](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6502 "6502")[8-bit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8-bit_computing "8-bit computing")[processor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Processor_(computing) "Processor (computing)") and can display text and two resolutions of color graphics. A software-controlled speaker provides one channel of low-fidelity audio. A model with more advanced graphics and sound, and with a [65C816](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65C816 "65C816")[16-bit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16-bit_computing "16-bit computing") processor, the [Apple II GS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_IIGS "Apple IIGS"), was added in 1986. It remained compatible with earlier Apple II models, but the II GS has more in common with mid-1980s systems like the [Atari ST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari_ST "Atari ST"), [Amiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiga "Amiga"), and [Acorn Archimedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes").

Despite the introduction of the [Motorola 68000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000")–based [Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macintosh_128K "Macintosh 128K") in 1984, the Apple II series still reportedly accounted for 85% of the company's hardware sales in the first quarter of fiscal 1985.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-libes198506-6) Apple continued to sell Apple II systems alongside the Macintosh until terminating the II GS in December 1992[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-7) and the IIe in November 1993.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-8) The last II-series Apple in production, the [IIe card for Macintoshes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_IIe_Card "Apple IIe Card"), was discontinued on October 15, 1993; having been one of the longest running mass-produced home computer series, the total Apple II sales of all of its models during its 16-year production run were about 6 million units (including about 1.25 million Apple II GS models) with the peak occurring in 1983 when 1 million were sold.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-autogenerated1-9)

## Hardware

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Apple_II&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Hardware")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Apple_iie.jpg/250px-Apple_iie.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_iie.jpg)

Apple IIe with DuoDisk and Monitor //

Unlike preceding home microcomputers, the Apple II was sold as a finished consumer appliance rather than as a kit (unassembled or preassembled). Apple marketed the Apple II as a durable product, including a 1981 [ad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising "Advertising") in which an Apple II survived a [fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire "Fire") started when a cat belonging to one early user knocked over a lamp.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-10)

All the machines in the series, except the IIc, share similar overall design elements. The plastic case was designed to look more like a [home appliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_appliance "Small appliance") than a piece of [electronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronics "Electronics") equipment,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-11) and the case can be opened without the use of tools. All models in the Apple II series have a built-in keyboard, with the exception of the II GS which has a separate keyboard.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Apple_IIc_with_monitor.jpg/250px-Apple_IIc_with_monitor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_IIc_with_monitor.jpg)

Apple IIc with monitor

Apple IIs have color and high-resolution [graphics modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_graphics "Apple II graphics"), sound capabilities and a built-in [BASIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BASIC "BASIC") programming language. The [motherboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motherboard "Motherboard") holds eight [expansion slots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expansion_slot "Expansion slot") and an array of random access memory (RAM) sockets that can hold up to 48[kilobytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilobyte "Kilobyte"). Over the course of the Apple II series' life, an enormous amount of first- and third-party hardware was made available to extend the capabilities of the machine. The IIc was designed as a compact, portable unit, not intended to be disassembled, and cannot use most of the expansion hardware sold for the other machines in the series.

## Software

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Apple_II&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Software")]

The [original Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_(original) "Apple II (original)") has the [operating system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") in [ROM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") along with a BASIC variant called [Integer BASIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_BASIC "Integer BASIC"). Apple eventually released [Applesoft BASIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applesoft_BASIC "Applesoft BASIC"), a more advanced variant of the language which users can run instead of Integer BASIC. The Apple II series eventually supported over 1,500 software programs.

When the [Disk II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_II "Disk II") floppy disk drive was released in 1978, a new operating system, [Apple DOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_DOS "Apple DOS"), was commissioned from [Shepardson Microsystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepardson_Microsystems "Shepardson Microsystems")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-Apple_DOS_commissioned-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-Apple_DOS_contract-13) and developed by Paul Laughton, adding support for the disk drive.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-Apple_DOS_developer-14) The final version of this software was Apple DOS 3.3.

Apple DOS was superseded by [ProDOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_ProDOS "Apple ProDOS"), which supported a [hierarchical file system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchical_file_system "Hierarchical file system") and larger storage devices. With an optional third-party [Z80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80")-based [expansion card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expansion_card "Expansion card"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-z80-15) the Apple II could boot into the [CP/M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") operating system and run [WordStar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WordStar "WordStar"), [dBase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBase "DBase") II, and other CP/M software. With the release of MousePaint in 1984 and the Apple II GS in 1986, the platform took on the look of the [Macintosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Mac_OS "Classic Mac OS") user interface, including a mouse.

Much commercial Apple II software shipped on [self-booting disks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-booting_disk "Self-booting disk") and does not use standard DOS disk formats. This discouraged the copying or modifying of the software on the disks, and improved loading speed.

## Models

### Apple II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Apple_II&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Apple II")]

Main article: [Apple II (original)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_(original) "Apple II (original)")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Micromodem_II_in_Apple_II.jpg/250px-Micromodem_II_in_Apple_II.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Micromodem_II_in_Apple_II.jpg)

An Apple II computer with an internal [modem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modem "Modem") and external [DAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_access_arrangement "Data access arrangement")

The first Apple II computers went on sale on June 10, 1977,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-Apple_II_intro_date-2)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-Apple_II_History-16) with a [MOS Technology 6502](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502") (later [Synertek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synertek "Synertek"))[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-17) microprocessor running at 1.023[MHz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertz "Hertz"), 4 KB of [RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory"), an [audio cassette interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_cassette_interface "Audio cassette interface") for loading programs and storing data, and the [Integer BASIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_BASIC "Integer BASIC") programming language built into the [ROMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read-only_memory "Read-only memory"). The video controller displayed 40 columns by 24 lines of monochrome, upper-case–only (the original character set matches [ASCII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII "ASCII") characters 0x20 to 0x5F) text on the screen, with [NTSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTSC "NTSC")[composite video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_video "Composite video") output suitable for display on a TV monitor, or on a regular TV set by way of a separate [RF modulator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RF_modulator "RF modulator"). The original retail price of the computer was US$1,298(equivalent to $6,900 in 2025)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-19) with 4 KB of RAM and US$2,638(equivalent to $14,000 in 2025) with the maximum 48 KB of RAM. To reflect the computer's [color graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_graphics "Apple II graphics") capability, the Apple logo on the casing was represented using rainbow stripes,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-21) which remained a part of Apple's corporate logo until early 1998. The earliest Apple IIs were assembled in [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley"), and later in Texas;[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-22)[printed circuit boards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printed_circuit_board "Printed circuit board") were manufactured in Ireland and [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore").

An external 5+1⁄4-inch [floppy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk") drive, the [Disk II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk_II "Disk II"), attached via a controller card that plugged into one of the computer's expansion slots (usually slot 6), was used for data storage and retrieval to replace cassettes. The Disk II interface, created by Steve Wozniak, was regarded as an engineering masterpiece for its economy of electronic components.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-24)

Rather than having a dedicated sound-synthesis chip, the Apple II had a toggle circuit that could only emit a click through a built-in speaker; all other sounds (including two, three and, eventually, four-voice music and playback of audio samples and speech synthesis) were generated entirely by software that clicked the speaker at just the right times.

The Apple II's multiple expansion slots permitted a wide variety of third-party devices, including [Apple II peripheral cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_peripheral_cards "Apple II peripheral cards") such as [serial controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_serial_cards "Apple II serial cards"), display controllers, memory boards, hard disks, networking components, and [real-time clocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_system_clocks "Apple II system clocks"). There were plug-in [expansion cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_processor_cards "Apple II processor cards") – such as the [Z-80 SoftCard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z-80_SoftCard "Z-80 SoftCard")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-z80-15) – that permitted the Apple to use the [Z80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80") processor and run a multitude of programs developed under the [CP/M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") operating system,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-z80-15) including the [dBase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBase "DBase") II database and the [WordStar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WordStar "WordStar") word processor. There was also a third-party [6809](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_6809 "Motorola 6809") card that would allow [OS-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OS-9 "OS-9") Level One to be run.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Third-party [sound cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_sound_cards "Apple II sound cards") greatly improved audio capabilities, allowing simple music synthesis and text-to-speech functions. Eventually, [Apple II accelerator cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_accelerators "Apple II accelerators") were created to double or quadruple the computer's speed.

[Rod Holt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Holt "Rod Holt") designed the Apple II's power supply. He employed a [switched-mode power supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switched-mode_power_supply "Switched-mode power supply") design, which was far smaller and generated less unwanted heat than the [linear power supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_power_supply "Linear power supply") some other home computers used.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-25)

The original Apple II was discontinued at the start of 1981; it was superseded by the [Apple II+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II+ "Apple II+").

### Apple II Plus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Apple_II&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Apple II Plus")]

Main article: [Apple II Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II_Plus "Apple II Plus")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Apple_II_Plus.jpg/250px-Apple_II_Plus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apple_II_Plus.jpg)

Apple II Plus

The Apple II Plus, introduced in June 1979,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-29) includes the [Applesoft BASIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applesoft_BASIC "Applesoft BASIC") programming language in [ROM.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") This [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft")-authored dialect of BASIC, previously available as an upgrade, supports floating-point arithmetic, and became the standard BASIC dialect on the Apple II series (though it runs at a noticeably slower speed than Steve Wozniak's Integer BASIC).

Except for improved graphics and disk-booting support in the ROM, and the removal of the 2k 6502 assembler to make room for the floating point BASIC, the II+ was otherwise identical to the original II. There are small differences in the physical appearance and keyboard. RAM prices fell during 1980–81 and all II Plus machines came with a full 48 KB of memory already installed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II#cite_note-30)
